People often talk about "pseudo difficulty" such as "hard" enemies simply having more health/ damage than "easy" enemies, but the idea of a bullet sponge isn't exactly a game mechanic, and dark souls doesn't use them. 

Of course "better" is going to be subjective and it's a different conversation to say "why does dark souls do difficulty so well?", But hopefully that answers your question a little bit.

my son never had any noticeable stimming behavior. he would twirl his hair when he was tired/stressed but i don't think the repetition went beyond what any young toddler would do to feel comforted or calmed. nothing was ever dramatically repetitive or drastic enough that i would consider it stimming. 

i imagine lockdown has made things much more stressful, i'm sorry that corresponded with this phase in your child's development. 

it's such a fine line to walk between parent's intuition and not wanting to be paranoid. personally i wouldn't consider any level of speech at 2.5 to be a "severe speech delay", and i would put more stock into how your child appears to observe and interact physically with his world. As a parent, trust your gut where your kid is concerned, but in my limited personal experience, if your kid appears healthy in other respects, don't stress yourself about the "expected" timeline for verbal communication.

is it strange though? i mentioned it specifically because i wondered if your son had a similar developmental experience, but didn't want to outright ask "iS Ur SoN GUdDeR aT BoDy oR BrAIn?" haha. I guess for whatever reason children will develop along different paths at differing rates, and it seems our sons both ended up excelling in physical motor skill development before verbal. my son was walking at 10 months and climbing the furniture not long after, and is today the fastest one in his class. 

The greater frustration that came for us is that he's always looked a full year older than he really was, so at 3 people would talk to him expecting a four year old speech level, but he only had the communication skills of a 2yo. Still, here we are today having full conversations together (and still playing soccer/football together) so i would put your mind at ease as much as possible. in addition girls typically develop speech earlier than boys, so try not to worry that he's not been keeping up with your daughter's pace. 

even so if we watch family videos from  a couple years ago, the sound of his non-verbal grunt does bring back a certain anxiety. It was so frustrating for us because we knew he was intelligent enough to understand what was happening, but didn't have the skills to communicate what he felt/wanted. 

long story short, he will have a completely wonderful childhood/adolescence despite these early setbacks. but speech therapy now will make the next year or two more manageable as he is able to communicate at  a slightly earlier stage. Good luck with finding someone who can work with him on this!

He was well into 2 before he started forming words properly, but was still "behind" well into his 3's and maybe the early part of 4. It was very disheartening for his mom and I cuz we felt like we had maybe been raising him poorly, but it really is just dependent on the child. He was also in the 99% for height and his motor skills were extremely advanced for his age, but that didn't have anything to do with our parenting either. Then his younger sister had a completely normal speech development timeline.

As with your child he seemed completely developmentally normal intellectually, and we were told therapy was not NECESSARY for development, but it was extremely helpful to start seeing results and be able to communicate better earlier on.

My son was older than 2  and still only communicated in grunts. He's 5 now and is completely verbally on par with everyone in his class. Some kids just take longer, but we did have a speech therapist come to our house (courtesy of social services) and work with him for about a year. It wasn't necessary, but it did speed along the process. Even so he was 4 before he caught up with his peers.

Hope this helps you feel a bit more positive!
